ccsTitle: Shortness of Breath, Weight Loss, Oily Stools — Office

patient.key: 3-year-old Caucasian boy. Triad: dyspnea + failure to thrive + steatorrhea. CXR: unilateral hyperinflation, pneumonia. Sputum culture: Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Sweat chloride / CFTR DNA would confirm. This is CF presenting with pancreatic insufficiency and chronic pseudomonal lung infection.

locationSequence.note: Kept in Office — should be inpatient

correctlyOrdered: Piperacillin-tazobactam — correct antipseudomonal penicillin for this resistant strain

missedOrders.why: The confirmatory test. Without it you have a clinical suspicion, not a diagnosis. CF is genetically confirmed — CFTR mutation on chromosome 7, most commonly delta-F508. Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L is diagnostic.

The oily stools are steatorrhea from pancreatic insufficiency. CFTR mutation blocks chloride transport → thickened secretions clog pancreatic ducts → enzymes can't reach the duodenum → fat malabsorption → failure to thrive. Pancrelipase (Creon) replaces the missing enzymes.
Patient was hypoxic with pneumonia. Oxygen is non-negotiable.
Bronchodilator before chest physiotherapy. Opens airways so mucus clearance is more effective. CF Foundation guideline.
Mechanical mucus clearance — percussion and postural drainage. Essential preventive measure in CF. The thick secretions don't move on their own.
Fat malabsorption means fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Every CF patient needs ADEK supplementation. Vitamin A (vision), D (bone, immune), E (antioxidant), K (coagulation).
Quantifies steatorrhea and confirms pancreatic insufficiency. The diagnostic test for the GI side of CF.
Patient has pneumonia + infection. Always get blood cultures before starting antibiotics. bacteremia changes management.
Ill-appearing child, likely poor oral intake. Dehydration worsens thick secretions — the CF cycle.
Most common cause of pneumonia in ages 3-5 is viral. Need to rule out before concluding CF is the only driver.
CF requires high-calorie, high-fat, high-protein diet with enzyme timing. Specialized nutritional management. This child is already malnourished.
CF is autosomal recessive. Parents need carrier testing. Genetic counseling for future pregnancies.
CF is a chronic multisystem disease. Pulmonary specialist manages airway clearance, infection surveillance, and pulmonary decline.
CF patients are particularly vulnerable to respiratory viruses. Annual flu shot is mandatory.
CF Foundation-accredited care centers provide multidisciplinary care — pulmonology, GI, nutrition, social work, genetics — with better outcomes than general care.
3-year-old with pneumonia, hypoxia, failure to thrive, newly diagnosed CF. Cannot manage in office. Location penalty: 50%.

optionalButNotGraded.why: Would show obstructive pattern. Not required but confirms pulmonary involvement rhythm.
Would be abnormal but culture was ordered — gram stain adds little beyond confirming infection
Good habit when giving IV fluids/meds — not tested
Noted as correct; pulse oximetry listed as missed — might be a grading overlap

teachingPoints: 65 roses = cystic fibrosis. The diagnostic triad in a toddler: pulmonary (SOB, hyperinflation on CXR) + nutritional (failure to thrive, low albumin) + GI (steatorrhea, oily stools from pancreatic insufficiency).

CFTR mutation disrupts chloride transport → secretions are thick and dehydrated in lungs (recurrent infections, bronchiectasis), pancreas (ductal obstruction → enzyme deficiency), and sweat glands (elevated sweat chloride — the diagnostic test).

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the signature CF pathogen. This strain was resistant to ceftazidime, gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, and ciprofloxacin — the antipseudomonal penicillins (piperacillin-tazobactam) or carbapenems (meropenem) were correct.
Pancreatic enzymes must be given WITH every meal and snack. Without them, dietary fat passes through undigested — the oily stools and failure to thrive you saw.
Preventive care in CF is just as important as acute treatment: chest physio, ADEK vitamins, annual flu shot, CF care center enrollment.
